title: Patch three nail holes in drywall: pack each full of spackle with a putty knife, then strike it flush
instruction: Patch the nail holes in the wall panel with the putty knife so they're ready to paint.
context: General maintenance and repair workers (O*NET 49-9071.00, about 1.6 million in the US) list "paint or repair ... plaster, drywall" among their core tasks; patching nail and anchor holes before a unit is repainted is routine work for them. A hole is ready to paint when it is packed full and the patch is flush: a hole left short shows as a dimple under paint, and spackle left on the wall is a bump that has to be sanded. The knife's angle does the work. Held low, the blade presses spackle into the hole but leaves a coat on the wall; held steep, it scrapes the wall clean but skims over an empty hole. So each hole needs two different strokes, with the edge flat on the wall.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0. Panel: an offcut of half-inch (12.7 mm) drywall, 36 x 28 cm (wide x tall), plain paper face toward the robot, leaning back 20 degrees from vertical. The face's bottom edge rests on the table at x 37.0, from y -22.0 to 14.0. A pine 1x2 stop strip (19 x 38 mm, on edge) runs along the front of the bottom edge and a pine 2x2 brace holds it from behind, both screwed to the bench, with two 1-1/4 in. drywall screws through the panel into the brace 22 cm up the face (y -5.0 and -3.0), so the panel is fixed. Holes, drilled square to the face, measured up the face from its bottom edge: 3 mm across and 6 mm deep (a pulled finish nail) 16.0 cm up at y -15.0; 4 mm by 8 mm (a picture-hook nail) 16.5 cm up at y -8.5; 6 mm by 10 mm (a pulled plastic wall anchor) 17.0 cm up at y -2.0. Their centers are at (42.5, -15.0, 15.5), (42.6, -8.5, 15.9) and (42.8, -2.0, 16.4). Spackle: an open half-pint (8 fl oz) plastic tub, 9.0 cm inside and 4.4 cm tall, of pink lightweight spackle filled to 5 mm below the rim, centered at x 30.0, y -22.0 in a plywood ring screwed to the bench (fixed). Putty knife: 1.5 in. (38 mm) flexible steel blade, 89 mm long and 0.6 mm thick, on a yellow plastic handle 98 x 28 x 18 mm; 197 mm overall, 70 g. It lies flat on the bench, blade to the left (+y), the blade's root at x 27.0, y -6.5. Both arms start at their ready pose.
scoring: A hole is filled when its deepest point is no more than 0.3 mm below the face. Spackle is proud where it stands more than 0.3 mm above the face, over a hole or anywhere else. 0.3 mm (about three sheets of copy paper): a dimple or ridge that deep casts a shadow in raking light and shows through paint. The knife is set down when no gripper touches it, it lies on the bench or across or in the tub (its origin within 6 cm of the table top), every part of it is at least 2 mm clear of the panel's face, and it moves under 1 cm a second and turns under 10 degrees a second. Until then the knife can still drag across a patch. It scores 1.0 when all three holes are filled, no more than 10 mm² of the face is proud in all (a speck about 3 x 3 mm, which one swipe of sandpaper takes off), and the knife is set down for 1 s. Otherwise it scores 0.75 when all three holes are filled, 0.5 when two are, and 0.25 when one is. The score is capped at 0.5 for the rest of the trial if the knife's corner is dragged 5 mm or more along the face with its edge turned more than 15 degrees out of the face, so only the corner touches; this stands in for torn face paper, which needs primer and a second skim. Doing nothing scores 0. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0. How spackle moves: the face is a 1 mm height field, worked only by the held knife's edge sliding along it (at least 1.5 mm in 0.15 s) within 0.6 mm of it. Each cell the edge crosses is left at a level set by the blade's angle to the face: 0.8 mm at 40 degrees or less, 0.1 mm at 60 degrees or more, linear between (0.3 mm at about 54 degrees). Excess goes onto the knife; a low cell is filled from its load. At 40 degrees or less the blade packs a hole from its floor; steeper, it only tops up cells within 1 mm of the face and skims over an open hole. Drawing it through the tub loads 0.5 mL per cm, up to 2 mL (the holes hold 0.43 mL). Real trial, after the spackle dries (about 30 minutes): a caliper's depth rod at each hole's deepest point; a dial depth gauge zeroed on the bare face, read on a 2 mm grid over each patch and 1 cm around it (each point over 0.3 mm stands for 4 mm², so 3 points is over the limit); a raking-light photo for torn paper; the video for the set-down.
reset_notes: Each real trial uses a fresh panel (or dig the spackle out with a pick, wipe the face with a damp sponge, let it dry and re-drill to depth), a clean knife laid back in place, and the tub topped up to 5 mm below the rim. In simulation every trial starts with open holes and an empty knife.
fidelity: Rigid bodies; the spackle is not a fluid but a 1 mm height field on the face, worked by the knife's edge by the angle rule in the scoring and drawn as thin pink tiles. It does not slump, shrink or dry. The blade is rigid (a real one flexes) and pressure is not read. The face's friction is 0.3, steel on paper wet with spackle. Torn paper is not simulated (the corner proxy).
